Hatchlings of the Desert spiny lizard emerge from eggs incubated at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] after approximately 90 days [ab = approximately 90 days], a developmental period that aligns closely with values reported for other phrynosomatid lizards of comparable egg size. At the moment of eclosion, neonates exhibit a snout-vent length of 3.2 cm [Lb = 3.2 cm] and a wet weight at birth of roughly 1 gram [Wwb = roughly 1 gram]. This modest body size at emergence reflects the substantial energetic investment required to produce a fully formed, yolk-dependent embryo within the parchment-shelled egg typical of the genus. The transition to exogenous feeding begins shortly after the hatchling emerges from the nest, at which point the young lizard must actively forage for arthropod prey to sustain its rapid early growth. Field observations indicate that the first few weeks of juvenile life represent a period of elevated vulnerability, as the small body size offers limited protection against predators and confers a narrow thermal safety margin in the arid habitats this species occupies.

As juveniles transition into the sub-adult phase, the Desert spiny lizard exhibits sexually dimorphic growth trajectories that become increasingly apparent with age. Females attain an ultimate snout-vent length of 10.7 centimeters [Li = 10.7 centimeters], a value that reflects the morphological constraints imposed by egg production and gravidity. In contrast, males reach a larger final adult SVL of 11.5 centimeters [Li = 11.5 centimeters], a pattern common among Sceloporus species where larger male body size is associated with enhanced territorial defense and competitive success during the breeding season. The ultimate wet weight for females scales closely with body length, reaching approximately 49.7 grams [Wwi = approximately 49.7 grams], while males achieve a corresponding adult mass of about 61.7 grams [Wwi = about 61.7 grams], a size dimorphism consistent with the energetic demands of reproduction and competition in this genus. Such divergence in adult body size is a well-documented feature of the reproductive biology of iguanian lizards.

Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species (14 °C [T = 14 °C]), the maximum reproductive rate reaches approximately 8 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 8 eggs per year], translating into roughly 1.5 clutches each year. Gravid females deposit between 4 and 24 eggs per season, but the exact number depends on maternal body size and resource availability. Females produce an average of 12 to 14 eggs per clutch, reflecting the substantial energetic investment in offspring production. Seasonal variation in prey availability modulates the timing and frequency of nesting events, with most reproductive activity concentrated in the spring and early summer months when arthropod abundance peaks. The parchment-shelled eggs, deposited in shallow burrows excavated in sandy soil, benefit from the moderating effects of subterranean humidity and temperature, which help maintain stable developmental conditions throughout the incubation period.

Sexual maturity in the Desert spiny lizard is attained after approximately 730 days since birth [tp = approximately 730 days since birth] when individuals are maintained at an average body temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. This relatively extended time to puberty reflects the slow pace of somatic growth and energy storage required before reproductive effort can be initiated. Young males typically begin showing territorial behaviors and developing the characteristic blue ventral patches shortly before reaching this threshold, while females begin vitellogenesis and follicular development around the same age. The onset of gonadal activity is tightly linked to seasonal cues, particularly photoperiod and temperature, which act in concert to trigger the hormonal cascade that culminates in mating and egg production. Captive-reared individuals maintained under constant thermal regimes show consistent timing of puberty, suggesting that the developmental program is robust to minor environmental variation. Field studies, however, reveal some plasticity, with lizards in warmer microhabitats occasionally maturing earlier, likely due to accelerated metabolic and growth rates.

Maximum lifespan records for the Desert spiny lizard indicate that individuals can survive for up to 5.9 years [am = up to 5.9 years] at 14 °C [T = 14 °C], placing Sceloporus magister among the moderately long-lived members of the Phrynosomatidae when compared to other small-bodied insectivorous lizards of similar body size. This longevity is likely facilitated by a combination of behavioral thermoregulation, refuge use in rocky crevices, and a relatively low predation rate in its preferred habitats. Senescence in this species is marked by a gradual decline in foraging efficiency and reproductive output, particularly among females, who may skip breeding seasons in their later years. The accumulation of ectoparasite loads and the wear of dentition have been proposed as proximate contributors to age-related mortality in wild populations. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this lifespan is consistent with the broader life-history strategy of the genus, which emphasizes repeated reproduction over several seasons rather than a single, high-investment breeding event, a trade-off that becomes particularly evident in older females who allocate fewer resources to clutches as they age, redirecting energy toward survival.
